title: Byblis
titleEn: The letter of Byblis, and the spring — Metamorphoses IX.530–665
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Byblis sends her brother Caunus a letter declaring that she loves him and asking him to take her as a lover. He reads part of it and drives the messenger off with a threat of death; she argues with herself about what she should have done differently, resolves to try again, and presses him until he leaves his country altogether. She follows him through Caria and Lycia until she collapses from exhaustion, and, weeping without stopping, is turned into a spring that still carries her name.

sentences.t:
“Quam, nisi tu dederis, non est habitura salutem,
hanc tibi mittit amans: pudet, a! pudet edere nomen.
sentences.l: “The well-being which, unless you give it, she is not going to have — this a lover sends to you: it shames me, ah! it shames me, to utter the name.
sentences.i: “The one who loves you sends you the health she will not have unless you give it. It shames me — oh, it shames me — to say my name.
sentences.n: A Roman letter opened with a formula of the type “A sends B salutem” — greetings, and literally safety or health. Ovid makes the formula the whole point: the salus she sends him is the one thing only he can give her. pudet is impersonal, “it shames (me)”, with no subject, and the interjection a is “ah”. She withholds both her own name and the word for what she is asking.

sentences.t:
Et si, quid cupiam, quaeris, sine nomine vellem
posset agi mea causa meo, nec cognita Byblis
ante forem, quam spes votorum certa fuisset.
sentences.l: And if you ask what I desire, I could wish that my case might be pleaded without my name, and that I not be known as Byblis before the hope of my prayers had been certain.
sentences.i: And if you ask what I want: I would rather my case were argued with no name attached, and that nobody knew Byblis until the hope of what she prays for was sure.
sentences.n: vellem is a potential subjunctive, “I could wish”, which softens the demand; posset agi depends on it with no ut, the bare subjunctive of wishing, and it is passive — “might be pleaded”. sine nomine and meo are pulled apart around the whole clause. nec cognita ... forem ... quam is “nor would I be known ... before”, and fuisset is a pluperfect subjunctive for the earlier point that never came.

sentences.t:
Esse quidem laesi poterat tibi pectoris index
et color et macies et vultus et umida saepe
lumina nec causa suspiria mota patenti
et crebri amplexus,
sentences.l: There could indeed have been for you an indicator of a wounded heart — my colour and my thinness and my face and often moist eyes and sighs set moving by no open cause and frequent embraces,
sentences.i: There could well have been a sign to you of the wound in my heart: my colour, my thinness, my face, my eyes so often wet, sighs with no visible cause, the constant embraces —
sentences.n: The long list joined by et ... et is the subject and index the predicate: all these things “could have been an indicator to you”. causa ... patenti is an ablative of cause wrapped around suspiria mota, “sighs set moving by no cause that showed”. poterat is imperfect indicative where English wants “could have been”: Latin puts the possibility in the indicative and leaves the unreality to the context.

sentences.t:
et quae, si forte notasti,
oscula sentiri non esse sororia possent:
sentences.l: and kisses which, if you happened to notice, could be felt not to be a sister's:
sentences.i: and kisses which — if you noticed at all — could be felt to be no sister's kisses:
sentences.n: notasti is syncopated for notavisti, “you have noticed”. possent has oscula as its nominative subject, and sentiri is a passive infinitive carrying its own predicate, “to be perceived not to be sisterly” — a nominative and infinitive, not the accusative and infinitive an active verb of perceiving would have taken. The neuter plural sororia agrees with oscula. The antecedent oscula has been pulled inside its own relative clause and stands after quae.

sentences.t:
ipsa tamen, quamvis animo grave vulnus habebam,
quamvis intus erat furor igneus, omnia feci
(sunt mihi di testes), ut tandem sanior essem,
sentences.l: I myself, however, although I had a heavy wound in my mind, although within there was a fiery madness, did everything (the gods are my witnesses) so that I might at last be more sound,
sentences.i: And yet I myself — though I carried a deep wound in my mind, though a fiery madness was inside me — did everything, and the gods are my witnesses, to be saner in the end.
sentences.n: quamvis here takes the indicative twice, habebam and erat, so the two concessions are stated as plain fact rather than granted for the sake of argument. sanior is the comparative of sanus, “more sound of mind”, not “healthier”: sanus of the mind is the standing opposite of the furor she has just named.

sentences.t:
pugnavique diu violenta Cupidinis arma
effugere infelix et plus, quam ferre puellam
posse putes, ego dura tuli.
sentences.l: and I fought long, unhappy, to escape the violent weapons of Cupid, and I have borne hard things, more than you would think a girl able to bear.
sentences.i: and I fought a long fight, poor wretch, to get clear of Cupid's violent weapons; and I have endured more hardship than you would believe a girl could endure.
sentences.n: pugnare with a plain infinitive, effugere, is poetic for “fight to escape”; prose would want a purpose clause. The comparison is built round an accusative and infinitive — plus quam ferre puellam posse putes, “more than you would think that a girl is able to bear” — and putes is a potential subjunctive, “you would think”. dura is neuter plural, “hard things”.

sentences.t:
Superata fateri
cogor opemque tuam timidis exposcere votis.
sentences.l: Overcome, I am forced to confess and to demand your help with timid prayers.
sentences.i: Beaten, I am forced to confess it, and to demand your help in frightened prayers.
sentences.n: superata is a perfect passive participle agreeing with the speaker, “having been overcome”, and cogor is passive as well: the sentence puts her at the receiving end of everything. fateri, by contrast, is deponent — passive in shape, active in sense, “to confess”. exposcere is stronger than asking; it is to demand insistently, an odd verb to stand beside timidis.

sentences.t:
Tu servare potes, tu perdere solus amantem:
elige, utrum facias!
sentences.l: You can save, you alone can destroy one who loves: choose which of the two you are to do!
sentences.i: You can save the one who loves you; you alone can destroy her. Choose which you will do!
sentences.n: solus is masculine, agreeing with tu, and belongs to both verbs: he alone holds both powers. utrum facias is a deliberative indirect question after elige, “which of the two you are to do”; the subjunctive carries the choice rather than futurity. amantem, “one who loves”, is her name for herself here and at the letter's opening, and the form does not mark gender.

sentences.t:
Non hoc inimica precatur,
sed quae, cum tibi sit iunctissima, iunctior esse
expetit et vinclo tecum propiore ligari.
sentences.l: It is not an enemy who prays for this, but one who, although she is most closely joined to you, seeks to be more closely joined and to be bound to you by a nearer bond.
sentences.i: It is not an enemy who prays for this, but a woman who, close to you as anyone can be, asks to be closer still, and to be bound to you by a nearer tie.
sentences.n: cum with the subjunctive sit is concessive, “although she is”. The whole argument turns on a superlative answered by a comparative: iunctissima is the kinship she already has, iunctior the thing she is asking for, and the Latin never has to say what the second kind of joining would be. vinclo is the syncopated form of vinculo, and ligari is passive, “to be bound”.

sentences.t:
Iura senes norint et, quid liceatque nefasque
fasque sit, inquirant legumque examina servent:
sentences.l: Let old men know the laws, and let them inquire what is permitted and what is forbidden and what is right, and let them keep the fine weighings of the statutes:
sentences.i: Let old men know the law; let them investigate what is allowed, what is sin and what is right, and let them keep to the balance-tongue of the statutes:
sentences.n: norint is the syncopated perfect subjunctive of nosco, for noverint, used as a jussive: “let them know”. The indirect question has three heads — quid liceat, quid nefas sit, quid fas sit: what is legally permitted, what is religiously forbidden, what is religiously allowed — and she is handing all three to somebody else. examen is the tongue of a balance, so legum examina is the exact weighing the law does.

sentences.t: conveniens Venus est annis temeraria nostris!
sentences.l: A reckless Venus is what suits our years!
sentences.i: A reckless love is what suits our age!
sentences.n: Venus stands for love itself. conveniens governs the dative annis nostris, “fitting for our years”, and nostris is “our”, hers and his together: she argues from a youth she claims they share, and the plural verbs of the next sentence keep it up. The weight of the sentence is on temeraria, rash and heedless of consequence, which is kept away from its own noun Venus and set down inside the dative pair annis ... nostris.

sentences.t:
Quid liceat, nescimus adhuc et cuncta licere
credimus et sequimur magnorum exempla deorum.
sentences.l: What is permitted, we do not yet know, and we believe that all things are permitted, and we follow the examples of the great gods.
sentences.i: We still do not know what is allowed; we believe everything is allowed; and we follow the example of the great gods.
sentences.n: quid liceat is an indirect question and takes the subjunctive; cuncta licere is an accusative and infinitive after credimus. sequimur is deponent — passive in form, active in sense, “we follow”. The three verbs are strung on et ... et so that the not-knowing, the believing and the following are offered as one single attitude, and the plural is the “we” of the young.

sentences.t:
Nec nos aut durus pater aut reverentia famae
aut timor impediet (tantum sit causa timendi!).
sentences.l: And neither a harsh father nor regard for reputation nor fear will hinder us (only let there be a cause for fearing!).
sentences.i: No hard father, no respect for our good name, no fear will stand in our way — only let there be something to be afraid of!
sentences.n: The singular impediet agrees with the nearest of its three subjects, which is normal in verse. The parenthesis is a jussive subjunctive of wish, tantum sit, “only let there be”, and causa timendi has a gerund in the genitive, “a cause of fearing”. What she is wishing for is the deed that would give her something to fear.

sentences.t: Dulcia fraterno sub nomine furta tegemus:
sentences.l: Under a brother's name we shall cover sweet thefts:
sentences.i: Under the name of brother we shall hide sweet stolen loves:
sentences.n: furta is literally thefts, and it is the standing word for a secret love affair; dulcia keeps the flavour of stolen sweetness. What she offers as cover is not a disguise they would have to build but the relationship they already have, and fraterno sub nomine sets the brother's name in the position of a roof.

sentences.t:
est mihi libertas tecum secreta loquendi,
et damus amplexus et iungimus oscula coram,
quantum est, quod desit?
sentences.l: There is to me the freedom of speaking secret things with you, and we give embraces and we join kisses in front of others — how much is it that is lacking?
sentences.i: I am free to talk with you in private; we embrace and kiss in front of everyone. How much is there still missing?
sentences.n: est mihi libertas is the dative of possession, “I have the freedom”. secreta is a neuter plural object of the gerund loquendi, “to speak secret things”, and coram, “in the presence of others”, is set deliberately against it. The closing question counts up what they already do and leaves the remainder unnamed.

sentences.t:
Miserere fatentis amores
et non fassurae, nisi cogeret ultimus ardor,
sentences.l: Have pity on one confessing her loves, and one who would not be going to confess, if the last burning were not compelling her,
sentences.i: Pity a woman who confesses her love — and who would not be confessing it now, if the last extremity of burning were not forcing her to —
sentences.n: misereor takes the genitive, so both participles are genitive and both are hers: fatentis, present, “confessing”, and fassurae, future, “about to confess”, under a negative. The nisi clause has the imperfect subjunctive cogeret, an unreal condition, so the confession is presented as something only compulsion could have produced.

sentences.t: neve merere meo subscribi causa sepulcro!”
sentences.l: and do not deserve to be written beneath on my tomb as the cause!”
sentences.i: and do not earn a place written on my tomb as the reason I died!”
sentences.n: mereor is deponent, so the imperative merere is active in sense — “earn”, “deserve” — and neve carries the negative into a second command. subscribi is passive, “to be written underneath”: a Roman epitaph could add the cause of death below the name. Her letter ends on her own grave, with his name standing on it.

sentences.t:
Talia nequiquam perarantem plena reliquit
cera manum, summusque in margine versus adhaesit.
sentences.l: The wax, now full, left her hand as it was ploughing such things in vain, and the last line clung on in the margin.
sentences.i: The wax ran out under her hand while it was still furrowing all this to no purpose, and the final line had to cling to the margin.
sentences.n: perarantem is a present participle in the accusative agreeing with manum, “her hand ploughing through”: perarare is to plough a field, and the stylus in wax is the furrow. plena and its noun cera are split across the line-end, so the reader meets “full” before learning what is full. summus versus is the last line written, forced round into the edge because the tablet had no room left.

sentences.t:
Protinus inpressa signat sua crimina gemma,
quam tinxit lacrimis (linguam defecerat umor),
sentences.l: At once she seals her own crimes with a pressed-in gem, which she wetted with tears (moisture had failed her tongue),
sentences.i: At once she seals her crimes with the stone of her ring pressed into the wax, and she wetted it with tears — her tongue had run dry.
sentences.n: The edition prints inpressa, not the assimilated impressa, and the spelling is kept. inpressa gemma is an ablative, the signet stone of her ring driven into the wax. deficio takes the accusative of the person it fails, so linguam defecerat umor is “moisture had failed her tongue”: she has no spittle to damp the seal and uses tears instead. sua crimina is the narrator's word here for what the tablets hold; she takes the same word up herself at 629.

sentences.t:
deque suis unum famulis pudibunda vocavit
et pavidum blandita “fer has, fidissime, nostro”—
sentences.l: and, full of shame, she called one from among her servants and, having coaxed the frightened man, “Carry these, most faithful one, to my—”
sentences.i: and, ashamed, she called one of her household slaves, and coaxed the frightened man: “Take these, most faithful of servants, to my—”
sentences.n: blandita is the perfect participle of the deponent blandior and is active in sense, “having coaxed”. blandior normally takes the dative; pavidum, the frightened servant, stands as an accusative object, one of the poet's freedoms with the verb. The verb of speaking does not arrive until the next unit, and the sentence breaks off on nostro, the word before the one she cannot yet say.

sentences.t: dixit, et adiecit longo post tempore “fratri.”
sentences.l: she said, and after a long time added, “brother.”
sentences.i: she said — and after a long pause added: “brother.”
sentences.n: The Latin holds nostro at the end of the previous line and puts fratri at the very end of this one, with longo post tempore, “after a long time”, measuring the gap between them. Grammatically the two words belong together, “to my brother”; the pause is the whole effect, and it is built out of the line-end.

sentences.t:
Cum daret, elapsae manibus cecidere tabellae.
Omine turbata est: misit tamen.
sentences.l: As she was giving them, the tablets slipped from her hands and fell. She was troubled by the omen: she sent them nevertheless.
sentences.i: As she handed them over the tablets slipped out of her hands and fell. The omen shook her; she sent them all the same.
sentences.n: cecidere is the poetic third-person plural perfect, an alternative to ceciderunt; the ending turns up several more times in these lines and is worth knowing on sight. elapsae is the perfect participle of the deponent elabor and is active in sense, “having slipped away”. Dropping what one is carrying was a real omen, and the narrator lets it stand with no comment beyond turbata est.

sentences.t:
Apta minister
tempora nactus adit traditque latentia verba.
sentences.l: The servant, having got hold of suitable times, approaches and hands over the hidden words.
sentences.i: The servant found the right moment, went to him, and handed over the hidden words.
sentences.n: nactus is the perfect participle of the deponent nanciscor and is active, “having obtained”. apta and tempora are split across the line-end with minister standing between them: the adjective is the second-last word of one line and its noun opens the next. latentia verba, “words lying hidden”, is exact rather than figurative: the writing is shut inside a folded and sealed tablet.

sentences.t:
Attonitus subita iuvenis Maeandrius ira
proicit acceptas lecta sibi parte tabellas
vixque manus retinens trepidantis ab ore ministri
“dum licet, o vetitae scelerate libidinis auctor,
effuge!” ait:
sentences.l: The Maeandrian young man, thunderstruck with sudden anger, throws away the tablets he has taken, with a part read by him, and, scarcely holding his hands back from the face of the trembling servant, “While it is allowed, you criminal instigator of a forbidden lust, escape!” he says:
sentences.i: The young man of Maeander's line, struck senseless with sudden rage, throws down the tablets the moment he has read part of them, and barely keeps his hands off the trembling servant's face. “Run while you can, you criminal instigator of a forbidden lust!” he says.
sentences.n: iuvenis Maeandrius names him by descent from the river Maeander; the narrator supplies the name Caunus at line 580. lecta sibi parte is an ablative absolute with a dative of agent, “with a part read by him” — he has not finished the letter. scelerate is a vocative adjective agreeing with auctor, and it is the hardest word in the sentence: he calls the messenger a criminal for carrying it, before he says anything at all about his sister.

sentences.t:
“qui, si nostrum tua fata pudorem
non traherent secum, poenas mihi morte dedisses.”
sentences.l: “you who, if your death did not drag our honour along with it, would have paid me the penalty with your death.”
sentences.i: “you who would have paid me for this with your life, if your dying would not drag our good name down with it.”
sentences.n: A relative clause taking up the vocative, so qui is “you who”. The condition is mixed: traherent is imperfect subjunctive for a state true now, dedisses pluperfect subjunctive for what would already have happened. tua fata, “your fates”, is a plural for your death. poenas dare, literally “to give penalties”, is the standing idiom for paying a penalty — in Latin it is the guilty party who gives.

sentences.t:
Ille fugit pavidus dominaeque ferocia Cauni
dicta refert.
sentences.l: He flees in terror and reports to his mistress the savage words of Caunus.
sentences.i: He runs off in terror and carries Caunus's savage words back to his mistress.
sentences.n: domina is the household word: she is the servant's owner, and the same noun comes back at the very end of the story. ferocia dicta is a neuter plural, “wild, savage words”, and the adjective is the narrator's judgment rather than any part of the servant's report. This is the first place in these lines where the Latin names the brother.

sentences.t:
Palles audita, Bybli, repulsa,
et pavet obsessum glaciali frigore corpus.
sentences.l: You grow pale, Byblis, the refusal having been heard, and your body, besieged by icy cold, is afraid.
sentences.i: You go white, Byblis, when you hear you have been refused, and your body shudders, under siege from an icy cold.
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside from the narrative to address his character directly; Bybli is the vocative of a Greek name. He does this again further on. audita repulsa is an ablative absolute, “the refusal having been heard”. The subject of pavet is corpus, so it is her body and not she that does the fearing, and obsessum, “besieged”, keeps up the language of an attack from outside.

sentences.t:
Mens tamen ut rediit, pariter rediere furores,
linguaque vix tales icto dedit aere voces:
sentences.l: But when her mind returned, her frenzies returned equally, and her tongue, the air being struck, scarcely gave forth such words:
sentences.i: But when her mind came back, the madness came back with it, and her tongue barely forced these words out into the beaten air:
sentences.n: rediit and rediere are the same verb twice, first in the ordinary perfect and then in the poetic third-plural form for redierunt, so that the return of the mind and the return of the madness are told in one and the same verb. icto aere is an ablative absolute, “the air having been struck”: the Latin idiom treats a voice as a blow struck on the air, and vix says how faint the blow was.

sentences.t:
“Et merito! quid enim temeraria vulneris huius
indicium feci?
sentences.l: “And deservedly! For why, reckless, did I make a disclosure of this wound?
sentences.i: “And I deserve it! Why, rash as I was, did I give this wound away?
sentences.n: merito is an ablative used as an adverb, “deservedly”, with the verb left out. temeraria is a nominative adjective agreeing with the unexpressed “I” — the Latin habit of using an adjective where English wants an adverbial phrase, “rash as I was”. It is the same word she used in her letter of the kind of love that suits their years.

sentences.t:
Quid, quae celanda fuerunt,
tam cito commisi properatis verba tabellis?
sentences.l: Why did I entrust so quickly to hurried tablets words which had to be concealed?
sentences.i: Why did I hand over to hurried tablets, so fast, words that should have been kept hidden?
sentences.n: celanda fuerunt is a gerundive with the verb “to be”, literally “were things having to be concealed”, which is the ordinary Latin way of saying “ought to have been hidden”. verba is the antecedent of quae but stands after its own relative clause. properatis tabellis is a transferred epithet: it was she who hurried, not the tablets.

sentences.t:
Ante erat ambiguis animi sententia dictis
praetemptanda mihi.
sentences.l: Beforehand the leaning of his mind was to have been tested by me with ambiguous words.
sentences.i: I should have sounded out first which way his mind leaned, with words that could be read two ways.
sentences.n: erat praetemptanda is a gerundive of obligation, and mihi is the dative of agent that goes with it: “was to be tested beforehand by me”. sententia stands near the end of one line and its gerundive praetemptanda opens the next, so the obligation lands only after the break. animi is a bare genitive, “the leaning of the mind”; the Latin does not say whose, and only the sense fixes it.

sentences.t:
Ne non sequeretur euntem,
parte aliqua veli, qualis foret aura, notare
debueram tutoque mari decurrere,
sentences.l: So that it should not fail to follow me as I went, I ought to have marked with some part of the sail what sort the breeze was, and to have run down over a safe sea,
sentences.i: To make sure the wind would follow once I was under way, I should have tried some corner of the sail to see how the breeze stood, and then run before it over a safe sea,
sentences.n: The whole of this movement of the speech is one sailing metaphor, kept up from here to line 594. ne non is the double negative of a purpose clause, “so that it should not fail to”. qualis foret aura is an indirect question with the older subjunctive foret for esset. debueram is a pluperfect indicative doing the work of “I ought to have”: Latin puts the obligation in the indicative and lets the unreality follow from the tense.

sentences.t:
quae nunc
non exploratis inplevi lintea ventis.
sentences.l: I who now have filled my sails with winds that were not scouted.
sentences.i: — I who have now filled my canvas with winds I never tested.
sentences.n: quae is a relative pronoun picking up the unexpressed “I” of debueram, “I, who”; it is feminine, so it can only be her. non exploratis ventis is an ablative, “with winds not reconnoitred”, and explorare is a scouting word taken from the same military and seafaring vocabulary as the rest of the image. The edition prints inplevi, not implevi, and the spelling is kept.

sentences.t:
Auferor in scopulos igitur subversaque toto
obruor oceano, neque habent mea vela recursus.
sentences.l: So I am carried off onto the rocks, and, capsized, I am overwhelmed by a whole ocean, and my sails have no ways back.
sentences.i: So I am swept onto the rocks, capsized, buried under the whole of the sea, and my sails have no way back.
sentences.n: Three passives in a row — auferor, subversa, obruor — keep her the thing being done to rather than the thing doing. toto and oceano are split across the line-end: the adjective closes one line and the noun stands second in the next, behind its own verb. recursus is plural, “returns, ways back”: a square sail cannot beat back against the wind, and that is the point of the image.

sentences.t:
Quid quod et ominibus certis prohibebar amori
indulgere meo, tum cum mihi ferre iubenti
excidit et fecit spes nostras cera caducas?
sentences.l: What of the fact that I was even forbidden by sure omens to indulge my love, at that time when the wax fell away from me as I was ordering him to carry it, and made my hopes liable to fall?
sentences.i: And what about this — that unmistakable omens warned me off indulging my love, at the moment when the wax dropped out of my hand as I was telling him to take it, and made everything I hoped for fall with it?
sentences.n: quid quod is an idiom for adding a further point, “what of the fact that”. prohibebar is passive and takes the plain infinitive indulgere, which itself takes the dative amori meo. mihi ... iubenti is a dative participle depending on excidit, “it fell away from me as I was ordering”. The play is in the two words of falling: excidit, “it fell out”, and caducas, “liable to fall”, so that tablets and hopes drop in the same breath.

sentences.t:
Nonne vel illa dies fuerat vel tota voluntas,
sed potius mutanda dies?
sentences.l: Was it not that either that day or my whole intention was to be changed — but rather the day?
sentences.i: Was it not that either the day or the whole plan had to be changed — the day, rather?
sentences.n: The gerundive mutanda stands once and does duty for each of the things named, and fuerat is the same past indicative of obligation as debueram in the lines before. She sets it out as a choice and then answers herself inside her own question: not the plan, the day.

sentences.t:
Deus ipse monebat
signaque certa dabat, si non male sana fuissem.
sentences.l: The god himself was warning and was giving sure signs, if I had not been badly sound.
sentences.i: The god himself was warning me and giving unmistakable signs — if only I had not been out of my mind.
sentences.n: male sana, literally “badly sound”, is a fixed way of saying out of one's senses: the adverb undoes the adjective. The si clause has the pluperfect subjunctive fuissem against two imperfect indicatives in the main clause, so the warning is stated as fact and only her madness is put in the unreal.

sentences.t:
Et tamen ipsa loqui, nec me committere cerae
debueram praesensque meos aperire furores
(vidisset lacrimas, vultum vidisset amantis!),
sentences.l: And yet I myself ought to have spoken, and not to have entrusted myself to wax, and, being present, to have laid open my frenzies (he would have seen my tears, he would have seen the face of one who loves!),
sentences.i: And yet I should have spoken myself, and not trusted myself to wax, and been there in person to open up my madness — he would have seen my tears, he would have seen a lover's face! —
sentences.n: debueram governs three infinitives, loqui, committere and aperire, and once again a pluperfect indicative carries the unreality. The parenthesis is a pair of pluperfect subjunctives, vidisset twice, an unreal apodosis with no protasis expressed: “he would have seen”. amantis is the genitive of the same participle she used of herself in the letter, so “a lover's face” is also “my face”.

sentences.t: plura loqui poteram, quam quae cepere tabellae.
sentences.l: I could have spoken more things than those which the tablets held.
sentences.i: I could have said more than the tablets had room for.
sentences.n: cepere is again the poetic third-plural perfect, for ceperunt, and capere here is “to have room for”, not “to take”. poteram is another past indicative doing the work of “could have”, the same construction as debueram and fuerat above.

sentences.t:
Invito potui circumdare bracchia collo
et, si reicerer, potui moritura videri
amplectique pedes adfusaque poscere vitam.
sentences.l: I could have put my arms around his unwilling neck, and, if I were being rejected, I could have seemed about to die, and could have embraced his feet and, poured out at them, demanded my life.
sentences.i: I could have thrown my arms round his neck, unwilling as it was; and if he pushed me away I could have looked like a woman about to die, and clasped his feet and, poured out at them, demanded my life.
sentences.n: invito collo is a dative with circumdare, and the adjective is transferred from the man to his neck: it is he who would have been unwilling. moritura is a future participle, “going to die”, so potui moritura videri is “I could have looked like a woman about to die” — she is planning the appearance. adfusa is a perfect passive participle, “poured out at his feet”, the posture of a suppliant; the edition prints adfusa, not affusa.

sentences.t:
Omnia fecissem, quorum si singula duram
flectere non poterant, potuissent omnia, mentem.
sentences.l: I would have done all of them — and if single ones of them could not bend his hard mind, all of them could have.
sentences.i: I would have done all of it; and if no single one of those things could bend that hard mind, all of them together could.
sentences.n: fecissem and potuissent are pluperfect subjunctives, the unreal past, while poterant in the if-clause is indicative: the failure of the single attempts is put as fact and the success of all of them together as the thing that never happened. duram and mentem are set as far apart as the two lines allow — the adjective at the end of one, its noun at the very end of the next — so “hard” hangs unattached across the break.

sentences.t:
Forsitan et missi sit quaedam culpa ministri:
non adiit apte nec legit idonea, credo,
tempora nec petiit horamque animumque vacantem.
Haec nocuere mihi.
sentences.l: Perhaps too there is some fault of the servant who was sent: he did not approach fittingly, nor did he choose, I believe, suitable times, nor did he seek out an hour and a mind at leisure. These things have harmed me.
sentences.i: Perhaps some of the fault is the servant's, the one I sent: he did not come up to him properly, did not pick the right moment, I think, did not look for a free hour and a mind at rest. That is what harmed me.
sentences.n: forsitan regularly takes the subjunctive, sit, “perhaps there is”. idonea and tempora are split across the line-end. vacantem agrees with animum: what he was to look for was an hour that was free and a mind free with it. nocuere is once more the poetic third-plural perfect, for nocuerunt. She has been blaming herself throughout the speech and here moves the fault onto the messenger.

sentences.t:
Neque enim est de tigride natus
nec rigidas silices solidumve in pectore ferrum
aut adamanta gerit nec lac bibit ille leaenae.
sentences.l: For he was not born from a tigress, nor does he carry hard flints or solid iron or adamant in his breast, nor did he drink the milk of a lioness.
sentences.i: For he was not born of a tigress; he does not carry hard flint or solid iron or adamant in his breast; he never drank a lioness's milk.
sentences.n: natus est goes with de tigride, “was born from a tigress”. adamanta is a Greek accusative singular of adamas, the hardest imaginable substance. The whole run is a set of stock reproaches for a hard-hearted lover, and she lists them as things that are not true of him — which is her ground for concluding that he can still be moved.

sentences.t:
Vincetur! Repetendus erit, nec taedia coepti
ulla mei capiam, dum spiritus iste manebit.
sentences.l: He will be conquered! He will have to be sought again, and I shall take no weariness of my undertaking, as long as this breath remains.
sentences.i: He will be conquered! He will have to be approached again, and I shall feel no weariness of what I have begun, as long as this breath of mine lasts.
sentences.n: vincetur is a future passive, “he will be conquered”, and stands alone as a whole sentence. repetendus erit is a gerundive with the future of “to be”, the same obligation construction as before but now pointed forwards. coepti is the perfect participle of coepi used as a noun, “the thing begun”. iste is normally “that of yours”; here it stands loosely for her own breath, her life, which is why the literal renders it “this”.

sentences.t:
Nam primum, si facta mihi revocare liceret,
non coepisse fuit: coepta expugnare secundum est.
sentences.l: For the first thing, if it were permitted me to call back what has been done, was not to have begun; the second is to storm what has been begun.
sentences.i: For the best thing, if I were allowed to undo what is done, was never to have started; the next best is to carry by storm what I have started.
sentences.n: primum and secundum rank two courses of action, “the first thing” and “the second”. liceret is an imperfect subjunctive in an unreal condition, “if it were allowed”, with the dative mihi. expugnare is a siege word, to take a place by assault, and its object is coepta, “the things begun”: she turns her own pursuit into a military operation. The shift from fuit to est puts the impossible option in the past and leaves the other in the present.

sentences.t:
Quippe nec ille potest, ut iam mea vota relinquam,
non tamen ausorum semper memor esse meorum,
sentences.l: For indeed he cannot — granted that I now give up my prayers — fail to be always mindful of the things I dared,
sentences.i: For even supposing I gave up now what I want, he still cannot help remembering always what I dared to do;
sentences.n: ut with the subjunctive relinquam is concessive, “granted that I give up”. The double negative nec ... non is the whole point: he cannot not remember. memor takes the genitive, ausorum meorum, and ausa is the neuter plural participle of the semi-deponent audeo used as a noun, “the things I dared”.

sentences.t:
et, quia desierim, leviter voluisse videbor
aut etiam temptasse illum insidiisque petisse;
sentences.l: and, because I shall have given up, I shall seem to have wanted it lightly, or even to have made a trial of him and to have gone after him with traps;
sentences.i: and because I shall have given up, I shall look as though I only wanted it half-heartedly, or even as though I were testing him and hunting him with a snare;
sentences.n: desierim is a perfect subjunctive in a causal clause with quia, which marks the reason as somebody else's rather than the speaker's own — the reason he would give. temptasse and petisse are syncopated perfect infinitives for temptavisse and petivisse. insidiae is an ambush, from hunting and from war, and petere is what one does to prey.

sentences.t:
vel certe non hoc, qui plurimus urget et urit
pectora nostra, deo, sed victa libidine credar.
sentences.l: or at least I shall be believed, having been conquered not by this god, who most greatly presses and burns my breast, but by lust.
sentences.i: or at the very least I shall be thought to have been beaten not by this god, who presses hardest and burns my heart, but by plain lust.
sentences.n: hoc and its noun deo are split across the line-end with the whole relative clause between them, so a reader waits a line to learn what “this” is. victa is a perfect passive participle agreeing with the speaker, and credar is passive too, so the whole sentence is about how she will be spoken of. plurimus is a superlative adjective doing adverbial work, “in his greatest force”. The distinction she is drawing is between being overcome by a god and being overcome by appetite.

sentences.t: Denique iam nequeo nil commisisse nefandum.
sentences.l: In short, I am now unable to have committed nothing unspeakable.
sentences.i: In the end, it is now beyond me not to have done something unspeakable.
sentences.n: The Latin is a deliberate double negative: nequeo, “I am unable”, with nil, “nothing”, and the perfect infinitive commisisse. What can no longer be done is the not-having-done-it. nefandum is literally “not to be spoken”, the strongest word available for a forbidden act, and she applies it to herself.

sentences.t:
Et scripsi et petii: temerata est nostra voluntas;
ut nihil adiciam, non possum innoxia dici.
sentences.l: I both wrote and asked: my will has been defiled; granting that I add nothing, I cannot be called harmless.
sentences.i: I wrote, and I asked: my will has been violated. Even if I add nothing to it, I cannot be called innocent.
sentences.n: et ... et couples the two perfects, “both wrote and asked”. ut with the subjunctive adiciam is concessive, “granted that I add nothing”. innoxia is feminine and stands as predicate to the passive infinitive dici, “to be called guiltless”. Magnus prints temerata est nostra voluntas, “my will has been defiled”; some editions print reserata, “has been unlocked”, which makes the line a matter of disclosure rather than of defilement.

sentences.t: Quod superest, multum est in vota, in crimina parvum.”
sentences.l: What is left over is much toward my prayers, small toward my crimes.”
sentences.i: What is still to come is a great deal added to what I want, and very little added to what I am guilty of.”
sentences.n: quod superest is the subject, “the part that remains”. The two phrases with in are of measure or reference: the remainder is counted first against her desires and then against her offences. The sentence is an accounting, and it is the reasoning she then acts on.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et (incertae tanta est discordia mentis)
cum pigeat temptasse, libet temptare: modumque
exit et infelix committit saepe repelli.
sentences.l: She spoke, and — so great is the discord of an unsettled mind — although it irks her to have made the attempt, it pleases her to attempt: and she goes out past the limit and, unhappy, brings it about that she is often driven back.
sentences.i: So she spoke; and — such is the war inside an unsettled mind — though she is sick of having tried, she wants to try. She goes past all measure, and the poor woman brings about her own repeated rejection.
sentences.n: pigeat and libet are both impersonal verbs, “it irks”, “it pleases”; the person they work on would stand in an oblique case, and here it is left unexpressed. cum with the subjunctive pigeat is concessive, “although it irks her”, against the indicative libet. committit repelli is “she brings it about that she is repulsed”, with a passive infinitive: the narrator makes her the cause of her own rejections. modum exit is “she goes out of measure”, a spatial way of saying she loses all restraint.

sentences.t:
Mox ubi finis abest, patriam fugit ille nefasque
inque peregrina ponit nova moenia terra.
sentences.l: Soon, when an end is lacking, he flees his fatherland and the unspeakable thing, and sets new walls in a foreign land.
sentences.i: Soon, when there is no end to it, he flees his country and the abomination, and lays out new walls in a foreign land.
sentences.n: patriam and nefas are both objects of the one verb fugit, so he flees the place and the thing together. nefas, “the unspeakable”, is the narrator's word here, and it echoes the nefandum she had just used of herself. ponere moenia is the standard phrase for founding a city; the text does not name the city he founds.

sentences.t:
Tum vero maestam tota Miletida mente
defecisse ferunt,
sentences.l: Then indeed they say that the sorrowing daughter of Miletus failed in her whole mind,
sentences.i: Then, they say, the grieving daughter of Miletus went out of her mind altogether,
sentences.n: Miletida is a Greek accusative, “the daughter of Miletus” — Byblis named by her father. ferunt, “they say”, with the accusative and infinitive defecisse, hands the report to tradition rather than to the narrator's own authority. tota mente is an ablative, “in her whole mind”, and deficere is to give out or fail — the same verb the narrator will use of the woods when they run out.

sentences.t:
tum vero a pectore vestem
diripuit planxitque suos furibunda lacertos.
sentences.l: then indeed she tore her dress away from her breast and, raving, beat her own arms.
sentences.i: then she tore the dress from her breast and beat her arms, raving.
sentences.n: vestem is held to the end of its line and diripuit opens the next, so the tearing arrives after the thing torn. plangere is the technical word for the ritual beating of the body in mourning, the gesture made over the dead; here she makes it for a brother who has only gone away. furibunda is from the same root as the furores of her speech.

sentences.t:
Iamque palam est demens inconcessamque fatetur
spem veneris, siquidem patriam invisosque penates
deserit et profugi sequitur vestigia fratris.
sentences.l: And now she is openly out of her mind, and she confesses the forbidden hope of love, since indeed she abandons her fatherland and her hated household gods and follows the tracks of her fleeing brother.
sentences.i: And now her madness is out in the open, and she admits to a hope of love that is not allowed — since she leaves her country and the household gods she has come to hate, and follows the footprints of the brother who has run from her.
sentences.n: palam est demens is “she is mad in public”, an adverb doing the work of a whole clause. fatetur is deponent and active in sense, “she confesses”; sequitur likewise, “she follows”. inconcessam is held back from its noun spem across the line-end. Magnus prints inconcessamque, which makes “forbidden” belong to the hope; some editions print inconcessaeque, which attaches it instead to the love. invisos penates is a hard phrase for the gods of one's own house.

sentences.t:
Utque tuo motae, proles Semeleia, thyrso
Ismariae celebrant repetita triennia bacchae,
sentences.l: And as the Ismarian bacchants, set moving by your thyrsus, offspring of Semele, celebrate the third-year festivals that come round again,
sentences.i: And just as the bacchants of Ismarus, set moving by your wand, child of Semele, keep the festival that returns every third year,
sentences.n: The narrator turns aside again, this time to address a god: proles Semeleia, “offspring of Semele”, is Bacchus, whom the Latin names here only by his mother and by his bacchae. motae is a perfect passive participle agreeing with bacchae, “having been set moving”, and tuo thyrso is the ablative that moved them. The trieteric festivals fell every third year by inclusive counting, that is every other year, and repetita marks their return.

sentences.t:
Byblida non aliter latos ululasse per agros
Bubasides videre nurus.
sentences.l: not otherwise did the young women of Bubasus see that Byblis had howled through the broad fields.
sentences.i: so — no differently — the young women of Bubasus saw Byblis howling across the wide fields.
sentences.n: Byblida is another Greek accusative, and the whole is an accusative and infinitive after videre, “they saw that Byblis had howled”. videre here is the poetic third-plural perfect for viderunt, not the infinitive — nurus is the nominative subject. ululasse is a howl and not a word: the simile gives the bacchants their festival and gives Byblis only the cry.

sentences.t:
Quibus illa relictis
Caras et armiferos Lelegas Lyciamque pererrat.
sentences.l: And these having been left behind, she wanders through the Carians and the weapon-bearing Leleges and Lycia.
sentences.i: Leaving them behind, she wanders on through Caria, and the weapon-bearing Leleges, and Lycia.
sentences.n: quibus relictis is an ablative absolute, “these having been left behind”, and quibus is a connecting relative: it looks back to the women of the sentence before and works as “and them”. Caras and Lelegas are Greek accusative plurals of the names of peoples, and the peoples stand for their territories. The prefix of pererrat does the work of a whole route: she wanders right through.

sentences.l: Already she had left behind Cragus and Limyre and the waters of the Xanthus, and the ridge on which the Chimaera had fire in her middle parts, the breast and face of a lioness, the tail of a serpent;
sentences.i: By now she had left Cragus and Limyre and the waters of the Xanthus behind, and the ridge where the Chimaera had fire in her middle, the chest and face of a lioness, and a serpent's tail;
sentences.n: quoque here is not the adverb “also” but quo with the enclitic -que, “and on which”, agreeing with iugo: the ridge is one more item in the list of places left behind. This trap is worth watching for — the same letters mean something quite different at the end of the tale. Cragon and Limyren are Greek accusatives. The Chimaera's three parts are given in three flat phrases held together by the single verb habebat.

sentences.t:
deficiunt silvae, cum tu lassata sequendo
concidis et dura positis tellure capillis,
Bybli, iaces frondesque tuo premis ore caducas.
sentences.l: the woods give out, when you, worn out with following, collapse, and with your hair laid on the hard ground, Byblis, you lie there and press fallen leaves with your mouth.
sentences.i: the woods give out — and there you, worn down with following, collapse; and with your hair spread on the hard ground, Byblis, you lie, your mouth pressing the fallen leaves.
sentences.n: The narrator turns to Byblis a second time and stays in the second person to the end of the sentence. lassata sequendo is “worn out by following”, with a gerund in the ablative. positis ... capillis is an ablative absolute, “her hair having been laid down”, interlocked word by word with dura ... tellure, the ablative saying where it was laid. frondes and caducas are held apart to either end of their clause, with tuo premis ore standing between the leaves and the adjective that says they have fallen.

sentences.t:
Saepe etiam nymphae teneris Lelegeides ulnis
tollere conantur;
sentences.l: Often too the Lelegeian nymphs try to lift her with tender arms;
sentences.i: Often the nymphs of the Leleges try to lift her in their soft arms;
sentences.n: conantur is deponent — passive in form, active in sense, “they try”. The object is not expressed at all and has to be supplied from the sentence before; some editions print illam here where Magnus prints etiam, which supplies it. Lelegeides is a Greek feminine plural adjective, the nymphs of the Leleges, the people whose land she has just been wandering through.

sentences.t:
saepe, ut medeatur amori,
praecipiunt surdaeque adhibent solacia menti:
sentences.l: often they instruct her that she should find a cure for her love, and they apply consolations to a deaf mind:
sentences.i: often they urge her to cure her love, and offer comfort to a mind that will not hear:
sentences.n: praecipiunt takes an indirect command, ut medeatur, “they urge that she remedy it”; medeor is deponent and takes the dative, amori. surdae menti is another dative, “to a deaf mind”, and that one adjective carries the whole failure: the advice is given and is not heard.

sentences.t:
muta iacet viridesque suis tenet unguibus herbas
Byblis, et umectat lacrimarum gramina rivus.
sentences.l: mute she lies and grips the green grasses with her own nails, Byblis, and a stream of tears wets the turf.
sentences.i: she lies without a word, gripping the green grass with her nails — Byblis — and a stream of tears soaks the ground.
sentences.n: herbas closes its line and Byblis, the subject of the whole sentence, opens the next, so her name arrives last of all. muta, “mute”, is set directly against the nymphs' talking in the line before. Magnus prints the nominative rivus, which makes the stream of tears the subject that wets the grass; some editions print the ablative rivo, which would make Byblis herself wet the grass with a stream of tears.

sentences.t:
Naidas his venam, quae numquam arescere posset,
subposuisse ferunt: quid enim dare maius habebant?
sentences.l: They say that the Naiads placed beneath these a vein that could never dry up: for what greater thing did they have to give?
sentences.i: They say the Naiads set beneath them a vein of water that could never run dry — for what greater thing had they to give?
sentences.n: Another accusative and infinitive after ferunt, “they say that the Naiads placed underneath”. his is a dative plural and the Latin does not say what it points to — the tears, or the grasses they are wetting — so the literal leaves it open. quae ... posset is a relative clause of characteristic with the subjunctive, “of a kind that could never dry up”. vena is the ordinary word for an underground channel of water. The edition prints subposuisse, not supposuisse, and the spelling is kept.

sentences.t:
Protinus, ut secto piceae de cortice guttae,
utve tenax gravida manat tellure bitumen,
sentences.l: At once, as drops come from the cut bark of a pitch-pine, or as sticky bitumen flows from laden earth,
sentences.i: At once — as drops come from the cut bark of a pitch-pine, or as sticky bitumen oozes out of heavy ground,
sentences.n: The first two of three similes, all of a solid giving up a liquid. secto ... cortice is an ablative with de, “from the cut bark”. The first clause has no verb of its own in the Latin: manat in the second serves both, and English has to supply one. gravida is “heavy, laden”, the word used of a pregnant creature, here of earth full of pitch.

sentences.t:
utve sub adventu spirantis lene favoni
sole remollescit, quae frigore constitit, unda,
sentences.l: or as, at the coming of the west wind breathing gently, water which had set hard with cold softens again in the sun,
sentences.i: or as water that has frozen hard softens again in the sun when the west wind comes breathing gently,
sentences.n: lene is a neuter adjective used adverbially with spirantis, “breathing softly”. Favonius is the west wind of spring. unda is the subject of remollescit but stands after its own relative clause, at the very end of the line, so the thing that softens is named last; the prefix of re-mollescit, “grows soft again”, holds the whole picture together.

sentences.t:
sic lacrimis consumpta suis Phoebeia Byblis
vertitur in fontem,
sentences.l: so, used up by her own tears, Byblis of Phoebus' line is turned into a spring,
sentences.i: so Byblis, of Phoebus's line, used up by her own tears, is turned into a spring,
sentences.n: consumpta is a perfect passive participle, “having been used up”, and vertitur is passive too: the change is done to her, not by her. suis, “her own”, makes the tears both the cause of the change and the substance of what she becomes. Phoebeia marks her descent from Phoebus, that is Apollo; the Latin gives the epithet and nothing more.

sentences.t:
qui nunc quoque vallibus illis
nomen habet dominae nigraque sub ilice manat.
sentences.l: which even now in those valleys has the name of its mistress and flows beneath a dark holm-oak.
sentences.i: which even now in those valleys carries its mistress's name, and flows out under a dark holm-oak.
sentences.n: Here quoque is the ordinary adverb, “also”, and not the quo with -que met a few lines earlier: nunc quoque, “now too”, ties the change to something a reader could still go and see. domina is the same word the narrator used of her when the servant reported back, and the spring is called Byblis. manat is the verb used of the bitumen in the simile, so the story closes on the word the comparison had prepared.
